sections.overview: This venomous viper inhabits arid parts of the Arabian Peninsula and adjacent Middle East, including Kuwait, southern Iraq, Jordan and western Iran.
sections.identification: It has a broad, flattened head, vertical pupils and often a small scale-like horn above each eye; unlike the related Saharan Horned Viper (C. cerastes), its eye projections angle backward and are commonly present.
sections.habitat: It is a nocturnal desert snake associated with sandy soils, sometimes where sparse vegetation provides shelter; regional accounts record it from broad sandy areas rather than a single dune type.
sections.diet: A stomach-content study in central Saudi Arabia found a mainly rodent diet, with beetles and lizards also represented; the result describes that sampled population rather than every part of its range.
sections.behavior: It is mainly nocturnal and its colouring can blend with different desert substrates; as a venomous viper it should not be handled.
sections.reproduction: The consulted ecological study examined diet and morphology, not breeding, so its reproductive cycle is left undescribed here.
sections.ecology: Its genus also includes C. cerastes and the Saharan Sand Viper (C. vipera); genomic work places C. gasperettii apart from the C. cerastes–C. vipera sister pair, despite their shared desert adaptations.
sections.conservation: The UAE national assessment lists it as Least Concern within the Emirates, but that regional 2018 assessment should not be presented as a current global IUCN category.
